## Measures can rank the same models differently

Most pages so far have scored models by the RMSE, with R² beside it now and then. Both are
**performance measures**: numbers that sum up how far a model's predictions fall from the
observed values. Each measure weighs the errors its own way, so two measures can rank the
same models differently, and a model can win on one by being wrong in a way the other
ignores. This page sets the common measures side by side, shows why they part on skewed
counts, and shows which of them can see predictions that are too low across the board.
Which one to report depends on what the predictions are for, which
[Choosing measures that match the objective](choosing-a-metric.qmd) sets out.

{{< include ../../_snippets/simulated-data.qmd >}}

{{< include ../../_snippets/python-tabs-run.qmd >}}

## Three measures weigh errors differently

A prediction's error is the observed value minus the prediction, the
[residual](../04-how-algorithms-learn/loss-functions.qmd) of one station. Each measure below
turns the errors of many stations into one number.

| Measure | What it is | What it minds most |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **RMSE** | the square root of the average squared error | large errors |
| **MAE**, the mean absolute error | the average size of an error, its sign dropped | every unit of error the same |
| **R²** | one minus the squared errors over the squared spread of the observed values around their average | the same errors as the RMSE, compared with predicting the average |

[Prediction and explanation](../01-introduction/prediction-and-explanation.qmd#rmse-measures-a-typical-miss-on-the-test-stations)
built the RMSE by hand, and MAE is the absolute error of
[Loss functions](../04-how-algorithms-learn/loss-functions.qmd), used here to score rather
than to fit. A forest fitted with squared error can be scored by MAE. For the RMSE and MAE,
lower is better. R² is 1 for perfect predictions, 0 for predictions no better than the
average of the observed values, and below 0 for worse. For counts, the Poisson deviance of
Loss functions is also used as a measure; it needs every prediction above zero, which
linear regression does not promise.

Each measure is at its best at a different prediction, as each loss is in
[Distributional assumptions](../06-assumptions-limitations/distributional-assumptions.qmd#each-loss-aims-at-a-different-middle-of-the-data):
the RMSE and R² when a model predicts the average of the values it could observe, MAE when
it predicts the median. For counts with a long right tail the median sits below the
average, so MAE favours models that predict low.

The **mean absolute percentage error** (MAPE), common in forecasting, divides each error by
the observed value. A count of zero makes it undefined, and on the other counts it punishes
a prediction that is too high far more than one that is too low, so it does not suit
counts.

## Software often reports the squared correlation as R²

This course reports the R² in the table above: `rsq_trad()` in yardstick and `r2_score()`
in scikit-learn. Many programs and papers report something else under the same name: the
**squared correlation** between the observed and predicted values, which is yardstick's
`rsq()`. For a linear regression scored on the data it was fitted to, the two are equal.
On new data, or for any other model, they are not, because the squared correlation asks
only whether the predictions rise and fall with the observed values. Predictions that are
all too low by the same proportion keep a perfect correlation.

::: {.diagram}
![Two definitions of R². Left, predictions in the right pattern but too low: the squared correlation is perfect, and R² is low because it counts the gap to the line where the predicted value equals the observed one. Right, predictions at the right level with scatter: both measures agree. The two definitions rank the two sets of predictions in opposite orders.](img/two-r-squared.svg){fig-alt="Two cards, each a scatter of eight predicted values against observed values, with a dashed line where predicted equals observed. Left, right pattern, too low: the points lie on a straight line of half the slope, below the dashed line; squared correlation 1.00, R² 0.17. Right, right level, scattered: the points sit above and below the dashed line; squared correlation 0.73, R² 0.70. A note says squared correlation asks how closely the points follow some straight line, whatever its slope, and R² asks how close they come to the dashed line: one minus the squared misses, divided by the squared spread of the observed values around their average."}
:::

## Worked example

Four models predict the survey's counts:

- **Predicting the average**: every station gets the average count of the fitted
  stations. It has no skill, and the other three should beat it.
- **Linear regression**, from
  [Linear and polynomial regression](../03-supervised-learning/linear-and-polynomial-regression.qmd),
  the simple baseline.
- **Random forest**, from
  [Random forests and boosting](../03-supervised-learning/forests-and-boosting.qmd).
- **Random forest on log counts**, the same forest fitted to the log of the count plus 1,
  each prediction turned back into animals, as in
  [Distributional assumptions](../06-assumptions-limitations/distributional-assumptions.qmd#training-on-log-counts-predicts-far-fewer-animals-than-were-caught).

Every model is cross-validated on the same ten folds of sites, and each measure is worked
out from the pooled out-of-fold predictions, as on
[Cross-validation](cross-validation.qmd). Every measure therefore scores the same
predictions of the same stations.

### Preparing the data

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| label: prepare
survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean() |>
  mutate(log_abundance = log1p(abundance))

set.seed(61)
folds <- group_vfold_cv(survey, group = site_id, v = 10)

inputs <- c("depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu",
            "substrate", "season", "longitude", "latitude")

with_inputs <- function(outcome, model) {
  recipe(reformulate(inputs, outcome), data = survey) |>
    step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) |>
    step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
    workflow(model)
}

forest <- rand_forest(trees = 500) |>
  set_engine("ranger", seed = 1) |>
  set_mode("regression")

average <- null_model(mode = "regression")
log_forest <- "Random forest on log counts"

models <- list(
  "Predicting the average" = with_inputs("abundance", average),
  "Linear regression"      = with_inputs("abundance", linear_reg()),
  "Random forest"          = with_inputs("abundance", forest),
  "Random forest on log counts" = with_inputs("log_abundance", forest)
)

# every station's out-of-fold prediction from each model, in the survey's order
out_of_fold <- map(models, \(model) {
  fit_resamples(model, folds, metrics = metric_set(rmse),
                control = control_resamples(save_pred = TRUE)) |>
    collect_predictions() |>
    arrange(.row) |>
    pull(.pred)
})
# back from log counts to animals
out_of_fold[[log_forest]] <- expm1(out_of_fold[[log_forest]])

predictions <- as_tibble(out_of_fold) |>
  mutate(caught = survey$abundance) |>
  pivot_longer(-caught, names_to = "model", values_to = "predicted") |>
  mutate(model = fct_inorder(model))

tibble(stations = nrow(survey),
       `average catch` = round(mean(survey$abundance), 2),
       `median catch` = median(survey$abundance),
       `stations with none` = mean(survey$abundance == 0))
```

## Python

```{python}
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer, TransformedTargetRegressor
from sklearn.dummy import DummyRegressor
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error, r2_score, root_mean_squared_error
from sklearn.model_selection import GroupKFold, cross_val_predict
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder

from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_survey_clean

survey = load_coastal_survey_clean()
caught = survey["abundance"]

folds = GroupKFold(n_splits=10, shuffle=True, random_state=61)

inputs = ["depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu",
          "substrate", "season", "longitude", "latitude"]
categorical = ["substrate", "season"]
numeric = [c for c in inputs if c not in categorical]

def with_inputs(model):
    recipe = ColumnTransformer([
        ("numeric", SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), numeric),
        ("nominal", OneHotEncoder(drop="first", sparse_output=False), categorical),
    ])
    return Pipeline([("recipe", recipe), ("model", model)])

# max_features="sqrt" draws a few inputs at each question, as ranger does.
forest = RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=500, max_features="sqrt",
                               min_samples_leaf=5, random_state=1)

models = {
    "Predicting the average": DummyRegressor(),
    "Linear regression": LinearRegression(),
    "Random forest": forest,
    # fitted to log counts, each prediction turned back into animals
    "Random forest on log counts": TransformedTargetRegressor(
        forest, func=np.log1p, inverse_func=np.expm1),
}

# every station's out-of-fold prediction from each model, in the survey's order
out_of_fold = {name: cross_val_predict(with_inputs(model), survey[inputs], caught,
                                       cv=folds, groups=survey["site_id"])
               for name, model in models.items()}

predictions = (pd.DataFrame(out_of_fold).assign(caught=caught)
               .melt(id_vars="caught", var_name="model", value_name="predicted"))

pd.DataFrame({"stations": [len(survey)],
              "average catch": [round(caught.mean(), 2)],
              "median catch": [caught.median()],
              "stations with none": [(caught == 0).mean()]})
```

:::

```{r}
#| label: helpers
#| include: false
f2 <- function(x) sprintf("%.2f", x)
f3 <- function(x) sub("^-", "−", sprintf("%.3f", x))
pct <- function(x) scales::percent(x, accuracy = 1)
```

The counts are skewed: the average station caught `r f2(mean(survey$abundance))` animals,
the median station `r median(survey$abundance)`, and `r pct(mean(survey$abundance == 0))`
of the stations caught none.

### RMSE and MAE choose different forests

The last column adds up each model's predictions over all the stations and divides by the
number of animals caught: 1 means the model predicts the right total.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| label: measures
scores <- predictions |>
  summarise(RMSE = rmse_vec(caught, predicted),
            MAE = mae_vec(caught, predicted),
            `predicted / caught` = sum(predicted) / sum(caught),
            .by = model)

scores |> mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 2)))
```

## Python

```{python}
scores = (predictions.groupby("model", sort=False)
          .apply(lambda g: pd.Series({
              "RMSE": root_mean_squared_error(g.caught, g.predicted),
              "MAE": mean_absolute_error(g.caught, g.predicted),
              "predicted / caught": g.predicted.sum() / g.caught.sum(),
          }), include_groups=False)
          .reset_index())

scores.round(2)
```

:::

```{r}
#| label: measure-numbers
#| include: false
score_of <- function(name, measure) scores[[measure]][scores$model == name]
best_on <- function(measure) as.character(scores$model[which.min(scores[[measure]])])
rmse_rank <- rank(scores$RMSE)[scores$model == log_forest]
ahead <- as.character(scores$model[scores$RMSE < score_of(log_forest, "RMSE")])
```

The RMSE picks the `r str_to_lower(best_on("RMSE"))`, at
`r f2(score_of(best_on("RMSE"), "RMSE"))`. MAE picks the
`r str_to_lower(best_on("MAE"))`, at `r f2(score_of(best_on("MAE"), "MAE"))`, a model
that comes `r c("first", "second", "third", "fourth")[rmse_rank]` of four on the RMSE,
behind `r knitr::combine_words(str_replace(str_to_lower(ahead), "^random", "the random"))`.

The last column shows why. The forest on log counts predicts
`r pct(score_of(log_forest, "predicted / caught"))` of the animals caught; the other models
predict close to all of them. Fitted to log counts, it aims near the median catch, below
the average, as
[Distributional assumptions](../06-assumptions-limitations/distributional-assumptions.qmd#training-on-log-counts-predicts-far-fewer-animals-than-were-caught)
found, and MAE, smallest at the median, rewards exactly that. For a stock estimate or a
map total, MAE has picked the model that misses
`r pct(1 - score_of(log_forest, "predicted / caught"))` of the animals.

### The squared correlation cannot see the shortfall

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| label: r-squared
r_squared <- predictions |>
  summarise(`squared correlation` = rsq_vec(caught, predicted),
            `R²` = rsq_trad_vec(caught, predicted),
            .by = model)

r_squared |> mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3)))
```

## Python

```{python}
r_squared = (predictions.groupby("model", sort=False)
             .apply(lambda g: pd.Series({
                 # yardstick's rsq() is the squared correlation,
                 # and its rsq_trad() is r2_score()
                 "squared correlation": np.corrcoef(g.caught, g.predicted)[0, 1] ** 2,
                 "R²": r2_score(g.caught, g.predicted),
             }), include_groups=False)
             .reset_index())

r_squared.round(3)
```

:::

```{r}
#| label: r-squared-numbers
#| include: false
r2_of <- function(name, measure) r_squared[[measure]][r_squared$model == name]
fitted_models <- setdiff(levels(predictions$model), "Predicting the average")
r2_rank <- rank(-r_squared$`R²`[r_squared$model %in% fitted_models])[
  fitted_models == log_forest]
```

The forest on log counts has a squared correlation of
`r f3(r2_of(log_forest, "squared correlation"))`, about as high as the random forest's
`r f3(r2_of("Random forest", "squared correlation"))`: its predictions rise and fall with
the catch as well as any model's do. Its R² is `r f3(r2_of(log_forest, "R²"))`,
`r c("the highest", "the second", "the lowest")[r2_rank]` of the three fitted models,
because R² also counts how far below the catch they sit. This is the left card of the
diagram above, in real predictions. Predicting the average scores an R² of
`r f3(r2_of("Predicting the average", "R²"))`, about zero, as R² is defined against it.

## Key points

::: {.key-points}
- **Performance measures** weigh errors differently. The **RMSE** and R² are at their best
  when a model predicts the average of what could be observed, **MAE** when it predicts
  the median.
- On these skewed counts the RMSE picked the `r str_to_lower(best_on("RMSE"))` and MAE the
  `r str_to_lower(best_on("MAE"))`, which predicts only
  `r pct(score_of(log_forest, "predicted / caught"))` of the animals caught.
- The **squared correlation**, yardstick's `rsq()` and what much software reports as R²,
  cannot see predictions that are too low across the board. The textbook R²,
  `rsq_trad()` or `r2_score()`, can.
- **MAPE** is undefined for a count of zero and favours low predictions. Do not use it for
  counts.
:::

## Try it yourself

1. Add MAPE (`mape_vec()`) to the table, scored on the stations that caught something.
   Predict first: which model does it pick?
2. Multiply the forest on log counts' predictions by one number, chosen so that their
   total matches the catch of the fitted stations in each fold. How much do its RMSE, MAE
   and R² change?
